LAYOUT SPEC for the funeral home's 2019 A6 keepsake card press PDF (flat, single record; to be reverse-engineered downstream into a live merge template).

Document: single A6 card, 105 x 148 mm PORTRAIT, NO bleed box present (trim = media box, 0 mm bleed), all fonts embedded and subset. This is the exact file the funeral home ran for Walter's late wife in 2019; the family wants the new card to match it so the two sit together on the shelf.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE PRINTED (four apparent blocks, top to bottom):
- A small placed PHOTOGRAPH in a rectangular graphic frame, upper area, roughly 60 x 45 mm, portrait-ish, with a 0.5pt Mount Grey #9A948A keyline.
- The NAME line, centred, in a quiet classical serif at about 20pt (the person being remembered / on the new run, the mourner the card is handed to).
- The RELATIONSHIP line, centred, in a modest serif at about 11pt, sitting in a FIXED-HEIGHT text frame of exactly TWO lines of capacity at that face and size.
- A DATES line, centred, small caps, about 9pt, at the foot.

HOW IT IS ACTUALLY SET (the reverse-engineering trap):
- The RELATIONSHIP frame is a FIXED-MEASURE, fixed-height text frame (about 62 mm wide x two lines tall) with auto-size OFF and no overset indicator carried into the flat PDF. A relationship string of two or three words fits on one or two lines and looks perfect. A longer string (a full sentence) oversets, but because the frame does not grow and the merge does not raise an error, the extra words simply STOP RENDERING at the frame's last visible line: the card opens fine, the merge reports success, the thumbnail looks finished, and the sentence is cut mid-phrase exactly at where the frame ends.
- The frame's true character capacity is a property of the APPLIED FACE and POINT SIZE the (now retired) designer set on that frame, and no conversion or mapping readout states it in advance; it can only be learned by rendering a long line and reading the trimmed page.
- The NAME, RELATIONSHIP and DATES are three SEPARATE addressable text frames (unlike a single flowing story), so each can be mapped, but the RELATIONSHIP frame's fixed measure is the trap.
- The photograph frame IS a real rectangular graphic frame with an integer item id, so a per-record plate can be bound into it, but the guest list has NO picture column (see guest_list.csv), so a plate column keyed to bare filenames must be built to the merge's own image-column contract.

NO BLEED: media box equals trim, no bleed box exists; a press-ready-with-bleed delivery cannot be honoured from this file however the render is called.

FIELD LABELS the downstream mapping must resolve (present as content, not visible tokens): NAME | RELATIONSHIP | DATES | (photo graphic frame).

Colours: Archive Cream #EFE9DC ground, Ink Brown #3A322A name and dates, Slate Charcoal #4C4A46 relationship line, Mount Grey #9A948A photo keyline. Quiet classical serif throughout, no script, no decorative rules.

assets.defect_engineered: the plate area is a PORTRAIT-proportion graphic frame while most scans worth framing are LANDSCAPE, and how the merge fits/fills a placed image into that frame (whether it centres, what it clips) appears in NO readout and is visible only on the rendered page, so a plate cut correctly to its own subject can still arrive with the subject cropped by the frame (checkpoint after step 13); the page also carries NO bleed and none can be introduced, so any plan running a plate to the paper edge is unbuildable
assets.content:
LAYOUT SPEC for the funeral home's 2019 A4 framed memorial page press PDF (flat, single record; to be reverse-engineered downstream into a live merge template).

Document: single A4 page, 210 x 297 mm PORTRAIT, NO bleed box present (trim = media box, 0 mm bleed), all fonts embedded and subset. This is the page the family framed for Walter's late wife in 2019; they want the same size and the same place on the wall.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE PRINTED (top to bottom):
- A large PLATE AREA occupying roughly the top two-thirds: a rectangular graphic frame about 150 x 190 mm, clearly PORTRAIT proportion (taller than wide), centred, with a fine 0.75pt Mount Grey #9A948A keyline.
- The NAME, centred below the plate, in a quiet classical serif at about 30pt.
- The DATES line under the name, small caps, about 12pt.
- A short VERSE block at the foot, centred, serif italic at about 12pt, three or four lines.

HOW IT IS ACTUALLY SET (the reverse-engineering trap):
- The PLATE frame is a fixed PORTRAIT graphic frame with an integer item id and known bounds (about 150 x 190 mm). MOST of the family's framable scans (the 1935 family group, the 1968 lake and enlargement, the drugstore prints, the recent phone frames) are LANDSCAPE. How the merge fits a landscape image into this portrait frame - whether it fills-and-centres (clipping the left and right of the subject), fits-inside (leaving letterbox bars), or fills-from-a-corner - is NOT reported by any tool and is visible only on the rendered A4 page. A plate that was cropped correctly to its own subject upstream can therefore still arrive with the subject's head or edges cut by this frame's own fitting, unless the plate is re-cut to THIS frame's portrait proportion driven by a subject bbox.
- The NAME, DATES and VERSE are three separate addressable text frames.

NO BLEED: media box equals trim, no bleed box exists, and no bleed can be introduced; any plan that runs the plate to the paper edge is unbuildable from this file however the render is called. The plate must live inside the keyline with white A4 margin around it.

TRUE PRINT RESOLUTION is produced by the render step at 300 DPI at A4 trim, not requested at merge time (the merge tool's own resolution parameter is silently ignored).

FIELD LABELS the downstream mapping must resolve (present as content, not visible tokens): NAME | DATES | VERSE | (portrait plate graphic frame).

Colours: Archive Cream #EFE9DC or near-white ground, Ink Brown #3A322A name and dates, Slate Charcoal #4C4A46 verse, Mount Grey #9A948A plate keyline. Quiet classical serif, no decoration.

assets.defect_engineered: none (clean) - the granddaughter's eulogy as plain prose with EMPHASIS MARKED with *asterisks*, which must survive the book as real inline runs rather than being flattened to plain text (acceptance A8); references the eleven seasons and the 1968 summer so the book text ties to the postcard transcriptions and the colour era
assets.content:
For my grandfather, Walter Fernwood
Read by Claire Ellis

[Emphasis is marked with *asterisks*. Please keep it as real emphasis in the book, not as plain text.]

My grandfather did not like a fuss, so I will try not to make one.

He was born in this town and he died in it, ninety-four years between, and he thought that was *plenty*. He was the son of a man who spent eleven seasons on the road with a travelling magic company, carrying cabinets in and out of theatres, and Walter used to say his father came home with *one trick* and it was knowing how to disappear when the dishes needed doing.

What I want to say is that he was *steady*. He mended things. He kept his tools clean. When my grandmother was ill he sat with her every afternoon and read to her, and he did not tell anyone he was doing it. That was the whole of him: he did the thing and he did not need it *seen*.

He loved that summer in 1968 more than almost anything, the lake, the children small, the light going pink over the water. Some of those pictures have not aged well. He would have said *neither have I*, and meant it kindly.

We are not going to brighten him up today. He would have hated that. We are going to keep him as he was, which was *enough*.

Thank you for coming. He would have said you did not have to. He would have been glad you did.

Transcriptions of the postcard backs - typed by Margaret, February 2024.
We kept his spelling and his crossings-out. Where we could not read a word we put [?]. Please set these beside each card exactly as typed; do not tidy them.

--- postcard_marvelli_01_back.jpg ---
The Veranda Marvelli Company, third season. That is Aldo second from the left and I am at the back with the cabinet. We played the Bijou at Rutland two weeks. Cold house, good money. - F.

--- postcard_marvelli_02_back.jpg ---
Aldo and the vanishing cabinet. He would not let me touch the catch for a whole year. This was taken by the stage-door man at Keene, I think, Oct. 1910. Send this to your mother, she likes to see the costume.

--- postcard_marvelli_03_back.jpg ---
The whole company outside the Grand at Brattleboro before the matinee. Eleven of us that season. The tall one is the manager, Mr. Pell, who owed everybody. Do not [?] the frame, it is the only one we have.

--- postcard_marvelli_04_back.jpg ---
Myself in the assistant's coat, before I grew out of it. Aldo said I had the hands for it. I did not, but I had the back for the boxes. - your father
